questions.subject: SEMINAR

The promise is too modest to attract students.
The promise proves the course is excellent.

questions.explanation: A course cannot guarantee employment. The promise overreaches and sets up failure.

questions.stem: An over-promise about outcomes lands unevenly across students. Why does that matter?

answer.exemplar: Students with fewer resources bear the cost when the promise fails, so the harm is distributed unfairly.

questions.explanation: Over-promises do not fail evenly. Those with least support suffer most when expectations collapse.
questions.hint: Ask who bears the cost of failure.

options.text: The essays are shorter because grading is lenient.
Students skim and lack material to write about.
Students write less to save paper.
Shorter essays prove deeper understanding.

questions.explanation: An unmanageable reading load leads to skimming, which starves the writing of substance.
questions.hint: Ask what the load does to preparation.

Make it longer without changing its tone.
Rewrite it to invite questions and evidence.
Remove the opening entirely.

questions.explanation: Repair means reopening the thread. A longer or stronger closure still closes it.

A louder restatement at every meeting.

Some members never gain the experience or influence.

The excluded members prefer not to chair.

The question gets a better answer.
The original asker is silenced.
The asker feels more included.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A question that supplies its own answer
questions.learningObjective: Spot a question that begs its answer

stimulus.body: A seminar asks 'Why is the best method clearly the one we use?'

questions.stem: What is wrong with this question?

options.text: It has no correct answer at all.
It is too short to be useful.
It asks for too much data.
It assumes the conclusion it asks about.

questions.explanation: The question presupposes its answer. It cannot be investigated fairly.
questions.hint: Check whether the answer is assumed.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An opening that closes a thread
questions.learningObjective: Recognize an opening that closes a thread
questions.stem: A seminar opening declares the topic finished before discussion begins. What is the effect?

options.text: It energizes participants to disagree.
It shuts down the thread it pretends to open.
It proves the conclusion is correct.
It shortens the meeting productively.

questions.explanation: An opening that declares closure prevents discussion. It does not prove or energize anything.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reply is still possible.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Repairing an opening that shuts a thread
questions.learningObjective: Repair an opening that shuts a thread
questions.stem: How should a seminar repair an opening that shut a thread?

options.text: Add a stronger conclusion to it.
Make it longer without changing its tone.
Rewrite it to invite questions and evidence.
Remove the opening entirely.

questions.explanation: Repair means reopening the thread. A longer or stronger closure still closes it.
questions.hint: Ask what would reopen the discussion.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What enforcing a norm requires
questions.learningObjective: State what enforcing a norm requires
questions.stem: What does enforcing a seminar norm require beyond stating it?

options.text: A longer list of norms.
A louder restatement at every meeting.
A vote to approve the norm.
A mechanism to detect and respond to violations.

questions.explanation: Enforcement needs detection and response. Restating or voting does not make violations costly.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when someone breaks it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a rotating role distributes
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a rotating role distributes
questions.stem: What does a rotating chair role distribute among members?

answer.exemplar: It distributes the power and responsibility of running the discussion so no single person dominates.

questions.explanation: Rotation shares control of the discussion. It prevents one person from dominating.
questions.hint: Ask what power the role carries.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A rotation that does not reach everyone
questions.learningObjective: Spot a rotation that excludes some

stimulus.body: A seminar rotates the chair role among a subset of members, leaving others out.

questions.stem: What is the problem?

options.text: The subset becomes too skilled.
Some members never gain the experience or influence.
Rotation itself is always harmful.
The excluded members prefer not to chair.

questions.explanation: Partial rotation withholds experience and influence from some. It undermines the purpose of rotating.
questions.hint: Ask who never gets the role.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A redirect that also silences
questions.learningObjective: Recognize a silencing redirect
questions.stem: A chair redirects a question away from the member who asked it. What happens?

options.text: The discussion becomes more efficient.
The question gets a better answer.
The original asker is silenced.
The asker feels more included.

questions.explanation: Redirecting away from the asker removes their voice. It does not guarantee a better answer.
questions.hint: Track whose question it was.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Analyzing a redirect
questions.learningObjective: Analyze a redirect's effect
questions.stem: When analyzing a redirect, what should be examined?

options.text: Only the length of the redirect.
Only whether the new topic is interesting.
Only whether the chair is popular.
Whether it silences someone and whether that serves the discussion.

questions.explanation: A redirect must be judged on both its topic change and its effect on voices. Interest alone is insufficient.
questions.hint: Check both topic and voice.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Consensus where the record shows a split
questions.learningObjective: Spot false consensus in the record
questions.stem: Minutes record consensus, but the exchange shows a split. What is the problem?

options.text: The split is irrelevant to the record.
The record misrepresents what happened.
Consensus is always better than split.
The minutes are too short.

questions.explanation: Minutes must reflect the actual exchange. Recording consensus after a split misrepresents the discussion.
questions.hint: Compare the record to the exchange.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Minutes that record agreement after a split exchange
questions.learningObjective: Judge minutes recording false agreement
questions.stem: Why is it harmful for minutes to record agreement after a split exchange?

answer.exemplar: It erases the disagreement from the institutional memory, preventing future revisiting of the unresolved issue.

questions.explanation: Recording false agreement hides unresolved disagreement. Future readers cannot see what was actually contested.
questions.hint: Ask what disappears from the record.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A synthesis that flattens what it reports
questions.learningObjective: Spot a flattening synthesis

stimulus.body: A synthesis memo reports a heated dispute as a calm agreement.

questions.stem: What does the synthesis do wrong?

options.text: It proves the dispute never happened.
It adds too much detail.
It flattens the disagreement into apparent harmony.
It makes the memo too long.

questions.explanation: Flattening removes the texture of disagreement. It misrepresents what was at stake.
questions.hint: Ask whether the tension survives.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Keeping a disagreement visible in writing
questions.learningObjective: Keep disagreement visible in writing
questions.stem: How should a written synthesis keep a disagreement visible?

options.text: By summarizing only the common ground.
By declaring one position the winner.
By omitting the losing position.
By recording both positions and the point of contention.

questions.explanation: Visibility requires stating both positions and the contention. Declaring winners or omitting losers hides it.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader needs to see the dispute.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A summary reporting a position no one held
questions.learningObjective: Spot a summary attributing a nonexistent position
questions.stem: A summary reports a position no participant held. What is the problem?

options.text: It shortens the discussion helpfully.
It invents a view and misrepresents the discussion.
It proves the discussion was unclear.
options.misconception: blames participants for a faulty summary

options.text: It removes the need for minutes.

questions.explanation: Attributing a position no one held invents content. It misrepresents what was discussed.
questions.hint: Check whether anyone actually held the view.
